name: Fatima Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the payroll team at the head office of a clothing retail chain, about four hundred shops. There are six of us, and we make sure around nine thousand shop staff get paid right every month. I got the team lead job in March when my manager moved to the HR side, and I'm honestly still learning half of it. A normal day is fixing pay errors, answering emails from shop managers about overtime, and checking the payroll run before it goes to the bank.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters: if we get it wrong, someone can't pay their rent. What wears me out is month-end, when we're there till eight and the system always crashes on the last day. I live with my fiancé Daniel, who drives buses, and I send my mum a bit every month since my dad died. So savings are basically whatever's left on payday minus one, which is not a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, that's probably about right, it's a tool and not a miracle. At work I'd say let's use it for the boring bits and move on. I'm not one for big opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, payroll is full of routine checks, and even a small tool could do a lot of what my junior two do. If the company used that to not replace someone who leaves, our month-end would get harder, not easier. So I'd be fine, but I'd watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and try the AI checking tool once the finance team says it actually catches errors. I'd try to save a little for the wedding, which we've pushed back once already. And I'd ask to go on the payroll qualification course so I'm not the least qualified person in my own team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, a bit uneasy. The work's steady, but money's tight with my mum and the wedding. That was true before any AI talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if something goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the wedding fund, honestly, because the money to my mum doesn't stop. Daniel says we can just do the registry office, and I keep saying my mum would cry. Maybe she'd cry either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until finance proves it. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen a new system in a shop chain go wrong, and a whole region got paid twice. I'd rather be second and right, because if payroll's wrong, real people don't get paid.

say: I'd say AI is a **tool, not a miracle**, and that sounds about right.
I'd suggest using it for the **boring bits** and moving on.
think: A small tool could do much of what my **two juniors** do.
If leavers aren't replaced, **month-end** gets harder for those left.
do: Try the **AI checking tool** once finance shows it catches errors.
Save a little for the **wedding**, which we've already pushed back once.
Ask to go on the **payroll qualification** course.
feel: Mostly okay, but **uneasy** about tight money with her mum and the wedding.
S0.quote: I'd rather be second and right, because if payroll's wrong, real people don't get paid.
fieldNote: Her caution comes from **responsibility**: errors mean people can't pay rent.
Her money pressure is **family**, sending money to her mum after her dad's death.
The **wedding** is the first thing she'd sacrifice.

steps.text: Try the AI pay-checking tool once finance proves it works
Put fifty a month into the wedding fund
Ask her manager for a place on the payroll qualification course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be sensible and make sure people get paid right while it changes. At work I'd want the old checks kept until the new system proves itself. I'd say it calmly, because panicking helps nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, payroll is exactly the checking and planning on that card. If the software does the checks, my six becomes three, and maybe they don't need me if the HR manager oversees it directly. I'm new and still learning, so I'm not the obvious one to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly once the first teams have them working, and get good at spotting where they go wrong. I'd finish the payroll qualification so I've got something on paper. And I'd look at pay and benefits jobs at the council, which is the only other big employer near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can picture the meeting where they tell us the new structure. I'd be making a list in my head of what we'd cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on that list in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding first, then my phone contract, then the car if we had to, though Daniel needs it for early shifts. Money to my mum stays, that's not up for debate. I'd rather eat cheap than tell her I can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joy, who's been doing payroll for twenty-two years and knows every weird contract we've got. Joy (the longest-serving person on my team) is the one who'd catch the software's mistakes. I'd fight to keep Joy, even over myself maybe.

say: I'd say let's be **sensible** and keep paying people right during the change.
I'd ask to keep the **old checks** until the new system proves itself.
think: Payroll is exactly the **checking and planning** on the card.
A team of six could become **three**, and I'm too new to be the obvious keeper.
do: Use the AI tools properly once **other teams** have them working.
Finish the **payroll qualification** to have something on paper.
Look at **pay and benefits jobs** at the council.
feel: Anxious, picturing the **restructure meeting** in advance.
S1.quote: Joy (the longest-serving person on my team) is the one who'd catch the software's mistakes. I'd fight to keep Joy, even over myself maybe.
fieldNote: She ranks the household cuts clearly, and **money to her mum** is untouchable.
She'd adopt AI **once proven**, true to her steady nature.
She values **experience** over herself, which says a lot about her as a manager.

steps.text: Learn the AI payroll checks once two other teams use them
Finish the payroll qualification by next summer
Apply for pay and benefits jobs at the council
Put the wedding on hold and cut her phone contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is frightening and too fast, and the government should make companies keep people on while they sort it out. At work I'd keep the payroll running and try not to scare anyone. I'd probably cry in the car once, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd assume my job's gone in 2028, all of it. Payroll, checking, planning, emails: that's all thinking work. Daniel's bus driving has until robots in 2031, so for three years his job is our only safe one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the wedding plans and save everything I could, even fifty quid. I'd look at hands-on work that lasts a few years, maybe a care job or training as a bus driver like Daniel. And I'd talk to my uncle, who has a cash-and-carry shop, about whether there's any work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep thinking we'd go from two incomes to one, plus my mum. That's the bit that makes my stomach drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing at first, honestly. I'd keep sending the money until I couldn't. Then I'd ask my brother to take over for a bit, which would be hard because he's never done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really train as a bus driver?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, if it paid. Daniel loves it, and the depot always needs drivers. Three years of bus-driving wages before the robots is three years of wages. I'd take that.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and companies should keep people on meanwhile.
I'd keep **payroll running** and try not to scare the team.
think: My whole job is **thinking work**, so it's gone in 2028.
Daniel's **bus driving** is our only safe income for three years.
do: Cancel the **wedding plans** and save every spare pound.
Look at **care work** or bus driving that lasts until robots.
Ask my **uncle** if his cash-and-carry has any work.
feel: Alarmed, with a **stomach drop** at going from two incomes to one.
S2.quote: Three years of bus-driving wages before the robots is three years of wages. I'd take that.
fieldNote: She uses the **robot delay** sensibly, looking at hands-on work for herself.
Her partner's **bus job** becomes the household's three-year anchor.
Support for **her mum** would pass to her brother, which worries her.

steps.text: Cancel the wedding booking and get the deposit back
Apply to train as a bus driver at Daniel's (her fiancé's) depot
Ask her uncle about work at his cash-and-carry

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so let's plan. At work I'd ask HR for a clear timeline for each team. I'd be the sensible voice, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job still goes in 2031. But five years is enough to get a qualification and move into something with more people in it. I'd want to be out of pure payroll by 2029 at the latest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd use the AI tools at work and get good at them, because that's experience. I'd finish the payroll qualification and then look at an HR advisor course, since dealing with upset staff is still a people job. We'd do a small wedding next summer instead of the big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a normal kind of anxious. Five years is like having a deadline you can see. I can work with deadlines, that's payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is HR safe though? It's thinking work too.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, no. The letters and the policies, AI does that. But sitting with someone whose dad just died and sorting out their pay, I think people will want a person for that a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a smaller wedding upset your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for a week. Then she'd be happy we're not in debt. My dad always said never borrow for a party.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to plan**, so let's plan.
I'd ask HR for a **clear timeline** for each team.
think: My job still goes in **2031**, but five years is enough to move.
I'd want to be out of **pure payroll** by 2029 at the latest.
do: Use the **AI tools** at work to gain experience.
Finish payroll and start an **HR advisor** course.
Hold a **small wedding** next summer instead of a big one.
feel: Anxious in a normal way, like a **visible deadline** she can work with.
S3.quote: Five years is like having a deadline you can see. I can work with deadlines, that's payroll.
fieldNote: Five years turns fear into a **plan** she's comfortable with.
She bets that **sensitive conversations** stay human longer than paperwork.
Her late father's advice, **never borrow** for a party, shapes the wedding choice.

steps.text: Use the AI payroll tools daily to build experience
Start an HR advisor course after the payroll qualification
Switch to a small registry-office wedding next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning and no one should be caught out. At work I'd say let's build the training into everyone's development plan. Honestly, I'd be fairly relaxed about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be careful. Ten years means I'm thirty-seven when the thinking work goes, which is mid-career. That's fine if I've moved by then, and bad if I've just sat there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing payroll for now and get properly good at it, using AI when it's proven. In a few years I'd move toward HR casework or wellbeing, the human side. And we'd have the proper wedding, just saved for, not borrowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. The bigger worries are the ones I already have: money for my mum, money for the wedding. Ten years makes AI just one thing on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about kids differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd planned on kids around thirty, and I think we still would. I'd just want one of us in a job that lasts, and Daniel's has until the robots, so maybe that's fine. I'd want to be in the HR side by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this you'd actually welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Month-end without staying till eight. If AI did the crashing payroll system's job at month-end, I'd be happy. I just want to still be paid at the end of it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty of warning for anyone.
I'd want training built into everyone's **development plan**.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when the thinking work goes, which is mid-career.
It's fine if I've **moved by then**, and bad if I've just sat there.
do: Keep doing payroll and use **proven AI** where it helps.
Move toward **HR casework** or wellbeing in a few years.
Save for the **proper wedding** rather than borrow.
feel: Uneasy, with AI as **one worry** among money for her mum and the wedding.
S4.quote: If AI did the crashing payroll system's job at month-end, I'd be happy. I just want to still be paid at the end of it.
fieldNote: With ten years, her **existing money worries** loom larger than AI.
She'd welcome AI taking the **month-end slog**, as long as she's paid.
Family plans stay on track, anchored by her partner's **hands-on job**.

steps.text: Use AI checking tools once the finance team proves them
Move into HR casework within three or four years
Save monthly for the wedding instead of taking a loan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because we'd go to one income overnight, and my mum relies on me too. What would help is the company keeping people on with pay while we retrain, even for a year. And some help for families who support parents, because that money doesn't stop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people like me who send money home. A lot of us at work do. When people talk about savings, they forget some of our money already belongs to someone else, like the money I send my mum.

headlineQuote: When people talk about savings, they forget some of our money already belongs to someone else, like the money I send my mum.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old payroll team lead** at a clothing chain's head office, managing six people.
She lives with her fiancé Daniel, a **bus driver**, and sends money to her widowed mum.
She's careful and **practical**, adopting AI only once others prove it works.
She uses the **robot delay** sensibly, eyeing bus driving or care work in fast scenarios.
With more time she plans a move into **HR casework**, betting people stay human longer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her household drops to one income while her mum depends on her.
whatWouldHelp: Employers keeping staff on **with pay** during a year of retraining.
Help for families who **support parents**, since that money doesn't stop.
